complaints.problem: "That rescue story" has an unclear antecedent because the preceding trauma-bay vignette never establishes the rescue or its circumstances.
The Austrian drowning rescue is treated as known evidence but receives no identifying details or actual narrative, weakening the section's stand-alone clarity.
The examples transfer the lesson across domains, but nearly all resolve through the same named-owner move and do not test harder cases where ownership is explicit yet coordination still fails.
The closing sentence about practicing until the move feels routine is generic and adds no mechanism or consequence.

The correct option almost always repeats ownership, seam, handoff, dependency, or system language, while most distractors are obvious blame, punishment, work-harder, or lone-commander strawmen; answer positions are balanced, but conceptual guessing remains easy.
The chapter briefly says complexity does not excuse sloppiness but does not explore when a named owner is insufficient, when shared authority is necessary, or when centralized command is appropriate.
The fast and deep reads rely on lightly established characters and rescue references, so their stand-alone performance is weaker than the full read and key takeaway.

parsedReview.oneParagraphVerdict: The chapter teaches one strong, memorable move: diagnose the seam before blaming the people. Its imagery, cross-domain applications, concrete exercises, and repeated if-then guidance make the idea approachable and usable, and the mechanism is explained rather than merely asserted. It falls short of the professional shipping bar because the quiz mostly rewards recognition of signature vocabulary, the layered summaries contain underintroduced references, and the limits section does not test the named-owner prescription against meaningful failure cases. No defect is unsafe, factually demonstrable as wrong, app-breaking, or severe enough to make the lesson unusable, but the assessment and boundary work need another editorial pass.
